front: Approximate prevalence of bicuspid aortic valve in the general population?
Two most important non-valvular associations with BAV?
back: Coarctation of the aorta (30–50%) and intracranial (berry) aneurysms.

front: State BAV aortopathy dimensions on TTE.
back: Aortic root > 40 mm OR ascending aorta > 37 mm is abnormal. Growth rate typically 0.4–0.6 mm/year.

front: Which family-screening recommendation applies to BAV?
back: First-degree relatives should undergo echocardiographic screening — ~20–30% of first-degree relatives also have BAV.

front: List three associations of a subaortic membrane.
back: VSD, PDA, coarctation of the aorta, Shone complex, bicuspid AV, persistent left SVC, and pulmonic stenosis.

front: When should surgical excision of a subaortic membrane be performed?
back: When at least moderate aortic regurgitation has developed (from jet damage to the aortic leaflets). In young patients with non-calcified AV, repair is favored over replacement.

front: Genetic and cardiac features of Williams syndrome?
back: Elastin gene deletion (chromosome 7q11). Cardiac: supravalvular aortic stenosis (hourglass narrowing), supravalvular PS, peripheral pulmonic stenosis, and coronary ostial stenosis.

front: Name the four staged operations for hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
back: Wait — three stages: 1) Norwood (neonatal) — neo-aortic reconstruction using main PA + systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (modified BT shunt or Sano RV-PA conduit). 2) Bidirectional Glenn (SVC to PA, ~6 months). 3) Fontan (~2–4 years, IVC baffle to PA).

front: Where does coarctation of the aorta typically occur?
back: In the upper descending thoracic aorta, near the ductus arteriosus (or ligamentum arteriosum), just distal to the left subclavian artery origin.

front: What Doppler pattern in the descending aorta indicates significant coarctation?
back: Persistent antegrade DIASTOLIC flow with a saw-tooth (run-off) pattern distal to the obstruction, and a resting peak gradient > 20–30 mmHg. Absence of diastolic flow reversal proximally.

front: Most common form of interrupted aortic arch and its syndromic association?
back: Type B (between left common carotid and left subclavian) — most common. Strongly associated with 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome).

front: Why is a raphe important on a suspected bicuspid aortic valve?
back: A raphe (fibrous fusion of embryonic commissures) can make a BAV look trileaflet in diastole. The valve must be evaluated in SYSTOLE (during maximal opening) to accurately determine number of functional leaflets.
